title: Chapter 133 — Warranty & Service Coordination
intro: When something breaks, you become the customer's lifeline.

sections.title: Walking Them Through It
sections.content:
The customer does not know how warranty claims work. Walk them through it step by step. 'First, I need your model number and serial number — they are on a sticker inside the door. Second, I am going to call [manufacturer] and file the claim. Third, they will schedule a service technician within [timeframe]. I will give you the case number so you can track it.'

Do the work for them whenever possible. The customer should not have to navigate a manufacturer phone tree. If you can file the claim on their behalf, do it.

sections.title: Managing Expectations on Timing
sections.content:
Be honest about repair timelines. 'The manufacturer typically schedules service within 5-7 business days. Parts availability can extend that if they need to order something. I will follow up with you every [3 days] until it is resolved.'

Never promise a timeline you cannot control. But always promise communication: 'I will keep you updated even if there is nothing new to report. You will not have to wonder what is happening.'

sections.title: Keeping the Customer Informed
sections.content:
The worst thing you can do during a warranty repair is go silent. The customer sitting at home with a broken dishwasher and no updates imagines the worst.

Set a follow-up cadence: every 3-5 business days, send a text or make a call. 'Hi [name], just checking in on your service claim. The technician is scheduled for Thursday between 10 and 2. I will check in after to make sure it went well.'

The customer who feels informed through a slow process is patient. The one who feels abandoned becomes furious.
